name: Zoe Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the live-line crew for the coast district, which means we work on lines while they're still switched on, so hospitals and farms don't lose power. It's slow, careful work with insulated gloves and long fibreglass sticks, and you check everything twice. I'm also the depot's drone pilot, so on quiet days I fly the cliff-top lines looking for cracked insulators. I love the focus of live work, it's the only time my brain goes completely quiet. What wears me out is the paperwork after, three forms for every job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in Porthaven with my friend Kim, who's a paramedic, so between us someone's always asleep in the afternoon. I've got about five months saved. I use AI every day, for the forms, for studying the new robot specs, even for working out the best tide times to fly the drone. On weekends I've started doing drone surveys of roofs for a solar installer, just for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype? I'd be a bit surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was still worth it for the boring stuff, because it saves me an hour a day on forms. At the depot I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd post drone videos, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me. Live-line work is skilled and there's never enough of us. I'd keep the drone side business ticking over and maybe grow it a bit. My worry would just be my knees, since live work is a lot of kneeling in buckets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the live-line crew going, keep the weekend roof surveys, and put the extra into savings. I'd probably take the advanced drone licence this year because it opens up bigger survey jobs. Save toward a flat of my own by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. I'd still be the one holding a live wire on a cliff top while the hospital keeps its lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the weekend surveying bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month right now, sometimes four. It's not big, but it's mine, and the installer keeps calling. I like having something that isn't tied to one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your knees. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The older live-line guys all have bad knees by forty. That's partly why I'm building the drone side, so I have something for when my body says enough.

At the depot I'd keep **showing shortcuts** to others.
think: **Live-line work** stays skilled and in demand, and nothing changes for me.
My real worry is my **knees** from years of kneeling in buckets.
do: Take the **advanced drone licence** this year.
Save toward **her own flat** by thirty.
feel: **Calm** and happy, still doing the work she loves.
S0.quote: I'd still be the one holding a live wire on a cliff top while the hospital keeps its lights on.
fieldNote: She already earns **side income** from drone surveys and likes not depending on one employer.
Her worry is **physical wear**, not technology.
She uses AI **daily** in a practical, unfussy way.

steps.text: Keep running the live-line crew in the coast district
Grow weekend drone roof surveys for the solar installer
Take the advanced drone licence this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is roughly what I expect, honestly. It's started already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good for line work, because the forms and the planning go and we get to do the actual job. To the crew I'd say learn the new tools early or someone else will. Online I'd post about how drones and AI make line work safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's an opportunity. The thinking parts of my job, the forms, the planning, the inspection reports, move to software, and I already use it. My drone work becomes more valuable, not less. The people I'd worry about are the planners and the older guys who don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to train the crew on the new job-pack system in the first month. I'd push my manager to let me lead a drone inspection programme across the whole district. On the side I'd add AI analysis to my roof surveys, so the installer gets a report instead of just photos, and charge more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited. Slightly guilty, because I know some people won't feel this way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald, the old planner. He's been doing outage plans for thirty years with a pencil and a big map. I'd be the person training the software that replaces Gerald (her depot's old planner), and I'd hate that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much more would you charge with the AI reports?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe double. Installers want a report that says which roof faces are good and which tiles are cracked. If the AI writes it and I check it, that's a twenty-minute job that's worth a hundred and fifty.

steps.text: Train her crew on the new job-pack software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028, robots by 2031. That's very fast. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that linemen should be first in line to run the robots, since we know the lines. At work I'd keep the crew calm and focused, because live work and distraction don't mix. Online I'd post about the transition, practically, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The live-line work goes around 2031. My drone and AI skills buy me a seat in whatever team deploys the robots, I think. But I'm honest with myself, there might be ten seats for a hundred people. I'm probably in the top ten, but not certainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to my manager and ask to be on any robot pilot programme from day one. I'd put all my survey money into savings until I had eight months. I'd also buy a second, better drone and grow the survey business while it's still something people pay a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit tense, but focused. It's like live work: you don't panic, you check everything twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the survey business is something people pay a person for. For how long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until the installers get their own AI drones, maybe 2029 or 2030. So it's a bridge, not a future. My drone business has a three-year shelf life in this picture, and I'd squeeze every penny out of those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you're not in the top ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have eight months saved and a few years of experience with drones and AI, which is more than most. I'd move wherever the robot work is. I'm single, I can move.

Online I'd post **practical** transition advice, not doom.
think: There may be **ten seats** for a hundred people, and I'm likely but not certainly in.

fieldNote: She expects to **keep an income** through robot work, though not guaranteed.

steps.text: Ask her manager for a place on the robot pilot programme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031 and 2034. That's comfortable for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version to get right, and the company should start training robot crews now. At the depot I'd be the one setting up demos. Online, the same practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can build a real case for myself: lead the drone programme, then the first robot trials. By 2034 I'd want to be running a robot crew, not competing with it. Five years is long enough for me to stop being the best live-line worker and start being the person the robots report to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the drone programme within two years and do a part-time robotics course from 2029. I'd keep the survey business but move it toward checking AI reports for installers. I'd buy a small flat in 2029 once my promotion was sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the quiet in my head during live work. Watching a screen while a robot does it won't feel the same. But I'd trade that for keeping my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The middle crews. Not the stars, not the people retiring, but the solid thirty-five-year-olds with kids and mortgages. They're too young to retire and too settled to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and 2039. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. To the crew I'd say plan your forties now. Online I'd post fewer opinions and more drone videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd do live work until my knees complain, then move into robot work in my mid-thirties on my own terms. The drone business might even grow into a proper company. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the live-line crew, grow the survey business, maybe hire a friend part time. Take the robotics course around 2032. Buy a flat in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of change I'd quite enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go full time on the survey business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, around 2030, if it's paying. I'd want a steady job underneath it first. I'm adventurous, not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people ignore it because it's far off. Ten years is the kind of warning people ignore until year eight, and then everyone panics at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there would be a scramble for the few robot jobs and I'd be competing with friends. What would help is the company being open early about how many robot roles there will be and how they'll choose. I'd rather know there are ten seats and fight fairly for one than find out the day the robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Live work is dangerous, and if robots do it, people stop getting burned. I don't think anyone should forget that part when they talk about job losses.

headlineQuote: I'd rather know there are ten seats and fight fairly for one than find out the day the robots arrive.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old live-line crew lead** and the depot's drone pilot on the coast.
She shares a flat with a **paramedic friend** and runs a weekend drone survey business.
She uses AI **every day** and sees most change as a chance to lead.
Even with AGI by 2028 she stays **uneasy rather than alarmed**, betting on robot roles.
She worries for **colleagues** like the old planner and mid-career workers with families.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because of a scramble for a few robot roles among friends.
whatWouldHelp: The company being **open early** about how many robot jobs exist and how people are picked.
